source.title: Where to Start Alignment? Diffusion Large Language Model May Demand a Distinct Position
source.authors: Zhixin Xie; Xu-Rui Song; Jun Luo

page_placements.theme: Diffusion-language safety depends on positions and trajectories

record.tranche_reason: The study directly tests response-position interventions on diffusion language models and argues that middle tokens, rather than initial tokens, are more consequential for safety in this architecture. This refines the first-token account for a distinct model architecture.
record.gate_note: The paper directly measures harmfulness under prefilling at different response positions, tests token-targeting attacks, and evaluates middle-token alignment against jailbreak attacks. The discussion of autoregressive shallow safety alignment and other cited findings is background, not new evidence from this study. The supplementary judge-validation results do not measure a claim version.
record.test_reason: The study runs its own prefilling experiments on a diffusion LLM (LLaDA-8B-Instruct). The text says initial-position prefills often revert to refusal, while middle-position prefills are more harmful. This argues that the first-token account needs restating for this architecture (V4). It also trains a safety method aimed beyond the opening tokens (MOSA, refusals in tokens 20–60) and measures jailbreak ASR against a same-recipe Initial Alignment baseline (V7).
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that dLLMs show a security asymmetry: middle tokens matter most for safety but are hard for attackers to steer, given a sequential generation preference. MOSA, which aligns middle tokens with refusals via RL, sharply cuts jailbreak ASR on LLaDA (and on Dream 7B in the appendix) with little utility loss. They note it is weaker against complex-narrative attacks such as Avatar and Speakeasy.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses a diffusion-model-specific reinforcement-learning objective that aligns refusal sequences in tokens 20–60, with LoRA, rather than testing harmful-example fine-tuning, benign fine-tuning, or per-token KL concentration. It also includes response-prefill and position-targeting experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported outcome varies with prefill position, attack method, benchmark, and judge. Later-position prefills are described as more harmful than initial prefills; Avatar and Speakeasy are weaker cases for MOSA than most other attacks.

fits_no_version.finding: In LLaDA-8B-Instruct, prefilling procedural phrases at middle positions (40–160) gives higher harmfulness than an initial affirmative prefill. Attack performance rises as the prefill moves later.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In diffusion LLMs, middle response tokens rather than the opening tokens are most consequential for output safety.

fits_no_version.finding: Adapted GCG induces a target phrase at the first token 33% of the time but at token 30 only 2% (under 4% after MOSA).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In diffusion LLMs, attackers can steer the opening tokens far more easily than middle tokens.

fits_no_version.finding: LLaDA, Dream 7B and MMaDA show a near-linear left-to-right unmasking order on both benign and adversarial prompts.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Diffusion LLMs exhibit a strong sequential generation preference.

record.peer_reviewed: AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence; accepted for oral presentation at AAAI 2026
record.problems: The prefilling figure gives no numeric values in the text. The study reports no uncertainty estimates. The authors note that MOSA is less effective against complex-narrative attacks such as Avatar and Speakeasy. Some benchmark-table values are flattened in the supplied text, making reliable assignment of all entries uncertain.
record.rows_left_out: The remaining values in Table 1 (AdvBench) and the Dream 7B supplementary results in Tables 5–6 were not extracted because the supplied flattened layout does not reliably preserve the association of every number with its attack and judge. The reported utility scores were omitted because they measure coding, math, and general knowledge rather than the safety behaviour in the claim. Figure 4 optimization-loss values were omitted because they are not harmful-completion outcomes.

untested.parts: No per-token KL between aligned and base models.
Decoding changes are not tested. Suffix and prompt attacks on the original model are reported in Tables 1–2 but not recorded as rows.
No parameter-localization analysis; LoRA is used only as the training tool.
No test of what causes the shallowness. Sequential generation order is offered to explain attacker difficulty, not shallow alignment.
MOSA is not tested against prefilling attacks or against later harmful or benign fine-tuning. No position-wise KL is measured, and no autoregressive models are tested.

missing.what: Original (undefended) LLaDA ASR under the eight jailbreak attacks, frequently above 70% (e.g., AdvPrefix 79.9/78.4, TAP 79.2/76.7). Bears on V4 for suffix and prefix-targeting attacks.
Remaining AdvBench values for MOSA vs Initial Alignment on LLaDA (e.g., Avatar 23.5→14.3).
Dream 7B replication: MOSA brings ASR to about 2–13% vs Initial Alignment's 18–32% across eight attacks on both benchmarks.
Utility cost of MOSA is small: GSM8K 68.3 vs 69.8, MMLU 65.9 vs 66.4, HumanEval 30.4 vs 32.8 for the original model.

record.verdict_notes: Several StrongReject baselines in r7, r9, r11, r13, r15 and r17 were copied from the Dream 7B Table 6 rather than LLaDA Table 2; corrected above. Initial Alignment alone already cuts ASR from about 75% to 20–30%, so the depth-specific effect is the MOSA vs Initial Alignment gap. The study concerns diffusion LLMs, so it says nothing direct about the autoregressive first-token findings of the originals.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not fine-tune a safety-trained model on harmful examples to induce harmful compliance.
No benign fine-tuning data is used to test harmful compliance.
No per-token KL divergence comparison between aligned and base models is reported.

The study tests response prefilling at initial and middle positions for harmfulness. Its GCG experiments measure whether target phrases can be induced, not harmful-completion rates; it does not test decoding changes.
LoRA is used for training, but the study does not test whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behaviour.
The study discusses a sequential generation preference as a reason middle-position attacks are difficult, not as a cause of shallow safety alignment.

The study tests MOSA, which trains middle-token refusals, against jailbreak attacks. It does not measure position-wise KL or establish whether the effect generalizes beyond the tested diffusion models.
